paragraphs.text: Five short conversations run down this page, and every one of them happens in a place you can point at: a trolley, a fish counter, a cheese counter, an aisle, a checkout. Listen once for the picture that fits, then read — the second reading is where the sentences start to stick.

The counter conversation is the longest and the most useful. Watch how many turns it takes before anybody says what they want: first who is next, then the offer, then the request, and only afterwards the extra item. {{de:Was möchten Sie?}} opens the transaction; {{de:Sonst noch etwas?}} invites the second sale. Learn the pair together and you can shop anywhere.
Sonst noch etwas? — Ja, ich nehme noch 150 Gramm Schinken. — Ist das alles? — Ja, danke.

paragraphs.text: German keeps small change and big money in two different words. Anything under a euro is counted in {{de:Cent}}; from one euro up you say the euro first and the loose change after it. The cashier's voice goes down at the end, so the number lands as a statement, not a question.
0,99 Euro → neunundneunzig Cent · 1,09 Euro → ein Euro neun · 2,20 Euro → zwei Euro zwanzig

You do not read the digits. A price tag written {{de:1,09 Euro}} comes out of your mouth as {{de:ein Euro neun}} — no zero, no comma, and {{de:neun}} where an English speaker expects ninety. The same habit shows up one line earlier in the page: the customer asks what something {{de:kostet}}, hears {{de:99 Cent}}, and only then asks about the second juice.

blocks.prompt: How does the cashier say this price out loud?

concept.title: Preise sprechen
concept.rule: Below one euro you say only the cents. From one euro upward you say the euro word first, then the loose change as a plain number; the leading zero and the comma are never spoken.
concept.exampleGerman: 1,09 Euro → ein Euro neun · 0,99 Euro → neunundneunzig Cent
concept.exampleEnglish: 1.09 euros → one euro nine · 0.99 euros → ninety-nine cents
